projects.title: Expense Tracker CLI
projects.summary: A real installable CLI that tracks spending, with budgets, CSV import and a plugin API.
requirements: `expense add --amount 12.50 --category food --date 2025-03-01` appends a record and prints its id; the amount is stored as integer cents or Decimal, never a float sum.
`expense list` supports --category, --since and --until filters and prints a stable, sorted table; `--json` prints machine-readable output.
`expense report --month 2025-03` prints totals per category and a grand total that equals the sum of the rows.
Data lives in a JSON file whose path comes from `--file` or `EXPENSE_FILE`; writes are atomic (write temp file, then os.replace) so a crash cannot corrupt it.
Exit codes: 0 success, 2 usage error (argparse default), 3 not found, 4 corrupt data file; errors go to stderr, results to stdout.
Invalid input (negative amount, bad date, unknown category when a budget is set) is rejected with a clear message and no partial write.
The package is installable (`pip install .`) and exposes a console_scripts entry point named `expense`.
deliverables: Installable package with pyproject.toml and console script
Test suite and README with usage examples
Built wheel/sdist uploaded to TestPyPI (Open tier: optional plugin API docs)

grading.tests: 25 pytest tests run the CLI through `main(argv)` and via subprocess: add/list/report paths, filters, JSON output and every exit code.
grading.quality: ruff check clean, mypy on the public API, pytest coverage >= 80% (pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80)
grading.deploy: Screenshot or log of `pipx install` from TestPyPI followed by `expense --help` running, plus the TestPyPI project URL.
hidden_test_ideas: Amounts such as 0.1 + 0.2 must total exactly 0.30 (no float drift)
Two adds in the same second produce distinct ids
A truncated JSON file exits 4 and is left untouched
Dates like 2025-02-30 and 2025-13-01 are rejected
`list` on an empty store exits 0 with an empty table, not a traceback

guided.receives: Scaffold: typed stubs with docstrings and TODOs, a README task list and a visible pytest suite that names every behaviour.
guided.does: Implement add/list/report against the scaffold, then add per-category monthly budgets: `expense budget set food 300` and a warning (exit code 0, message on stderr) when a month exceeds it.

spec.receives: A written spec (the requirements list) and the public interface only; a small visible smoke test. The full hidden test suite runs when you submit or in CI.
spec.does: Build the CLI from the spec, add budgets, then CSV import (`expense import bank.csv --map date=Date,amount=Amount`) that reports how many rows were imported, skipped as duplicates, or rejected.

open.receives: A one-paragraph brief and the review rubric. No tests are provided: you write your own and you decide the design.
open.does: Ship a CLI people could use for a real month of spending, with import and a plugin mechanism of your own design.
open.extension: Add a plugin system: discover exporters and importers through `importlib.metadata.entry_points(group="expense.plugins")` so a separate package can add `expense export --format ledger` without editing the core.
review_rubric: Correct money handling (integers/Decimal, rounding rules documented)
CLI ergonomics: help text, exit codes, errors on stderr
Robust persistence (atomic writes, corrupt-file handling)
Extensibility: the plugin boundary is small, documented and tested
Tests: behaviour-focused, no reliance on the real home directory

deployment.free_tier: TestPyPI and PyPI are free. Use an API token scoped to the project; TestPyPI is a separate account and index from PyPI, and its dependencies may be missing, so install with `--extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple`.
deployment.teardown: Delete the local venv and pipx install (`pipx uninstall expense-tracker`). Uploaded files cannot be re-uploaded with the same version; bump the version and delete the token when done.

hints: Keep the domain logic (records, totals, budgets) in a module with no argparse and no printing; the CLI is a thin layer, which makes the 25 behaviours easy to test.
Store cents as int. Parse user input with `Decimal(str)` and quantize; float addition is the classic hidden-test trap.
Have `main(argv=None) -> int` return the exit code and call `sys.exit(main())` only in `__main__`; tests then never need a subprocess for the common paths.
Use `tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(dir=same_dir, delete=False)` followed by `os.replace` for atomic writes.

projects.title: Text-Adventure Engine
projects.summary: A small interactive-fiction engine with a data-driven world that also runs in the browser.
requirements: A `Game` object holds the world state (current room, inventory, flags) and exposes `step(command) -> Response` with no direct print or input calls.
Commands `go <dir>`, `look`, `take <item>`, `drop <item>`, `inventory`, `use <item> [on <thing>]`, `quit` are parsed case-insensitively with unknown commands answered helpfully.
Locked exits and conditional descriptions are modelled as guards on transitions (state machine), not nested if-chains in the loop.
The world (rooms, exits, items, win condition) is loaded from a data file and validated: dangling exits, duplicate ids and unreachable win states are reported before play.
A save/load function round-trips the full state to JSON and a loaded game continues identically.
A scripted transcript (list of commands and expected substrings) can be replayed by a test helper and by the CLI `--script file`.
The same engine runs in the browser under Pyodide: the module is pure Python with no filesystem or terminal assumptions.
deliverables: Engine package with a sample world (at least 6 rooms and a winning path)
Terminal runner and a static page that loads the engine under Pyodide
Scripted-playthrough test suite

grading.tests: Visible tests replay 3 scripted walkthroughs (win, lose, dead end) and assert the transcript and final state.

grading.deploy: URL of the deployed page; the deploy check loads it and plays the scripted walkthrough.
hidden_test_ideas: A walkthrough that takes items in a different order still wins
Taking an item twice fails gracefully and does not duplicate it
A saved and reloaded game produces the same transcript as an uninterrupted one
A world with a dangling exit is rejected with the room id in the message
Random garbage commands never raise

Write the transcript replay helper before the engine; it keeps you honest about output stability.

projects.title: CSV/Log ETL Pipeline
projects.summary: A streaming CSV/log pipeline with rejects, golden-output tests and a hard memory ceiling.
requirements: `etl run --in access.log.gz --out out.csv` streams input line by line and never holds the whole file in memory; peak RSS stays under a cap for a 1M-row input.
Stages are generator functions composed in a pipeline (`parse -> validate -> transform -> aggregate`); each stage is testable in isolation.
Bad rows are diverted to a rejects file with a reason and line number; the run summary reports counts read/kept/rejected.
Output is deterministic: identical input yields byte-identical output (stable ordering, fixed float formatting).
Handles gzip transparently, UTF-8 with BOM, quoted commas and embedded newlines (csv module dialect handling).
Aggregations (group counts, sums, min/max) use bounded state; a `--top N` option uses heapq rather than a full sort.
Exit code is non-zero when the reject rate exceeds `--max-reject-rate`.
deliverables: CLI package and README
Golden-file test data (input and expected output)
Dockerfile that runs the pipeline

grading.tests: Visible tests compare output to golden files and run a memory-capped check (tracemalloc or resource.setrlimit) on a generated large input.
grading.quality: ruff check clean, mypy on the public API, pytest coverage >= 80% (pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80)
grading.deploy: Output of `docker run --rm -v $PWD/data:/data etl run ...` and `docker image ls` showing the image size.
hidden_test_ideas: A 2M-row generated file runs under the memory cap
Input with CRLF, BOM and quoted newlines gives the golden output
Truncated gzip fails with a clear error and exit code
Reject file contents match expected reasons
Stage functions are lazy: consuming 10 rows of a huge input does no more than ~10 rows of work

guided.receives: Scaffold: typed stubs with docstrings and TODOs, a README task list and a visible pytest suite that names every behaviour.
guided.does: Complete parse/validate/transform generators for a fixed column layout and get the golden output to match.

spec.receives: A written spec (the requirements list) and the public interface only; a small visible smoke test. The full hidden test suite runs when you submit or in CI.
spec.does: Build the pipeline from the spec and make it schema-driven: a YAML/JSON schema declares columns, types and rules; hidden tests use schemas you have not seen.

open.receives: A one-paragraph brief and the review rubric. No tests are provided: you write your own and you decide the design.
open.does: Turn it into a small streaming ETL tool that could process a day of production logs with strict memory bounds.
open.extension: Add streaming windowed aggregation (per-minute buckets emitted as the watermark passes) and an on-disk external sort for outputs that do not fit in memory.
review_rubric: Memory behaviour is proven with a measurement, not assumed
Pipeline stages are small, lazy and composable
Data quality handling: rejects, counts, deterministic output
Schema format is well designed and validated with good errors
Docs and tests show how to extend with a new stage

deployment.free_tier: Docker Engine and Docker Desktop for personal use are free; build locally. Use a slim Python base image, a non-root user and a .dockerignore.
deployment.teardown: `docker rm` the container and `docker image rm` the image; `docker system prune` for dangling layers.

hints: Every stage takes an iterable and returns an iterator; never call `list()` or `sorted()` on the stream unless you can justify it.
`csv.reader` over a file opened with `newline=""` handles quoted newlines; wrap gzip with `io.TextIOWrapper` or `gzip.open(..., "rt")`.
Measure memory with `tracemalloc` peak or `resource.getrusage`; assert in a test so a regression is caught.
For top-N use `heapq.nlargest` or a bounded heap; think about ties for determinism.

projects.title: Scraper + Cache
projects.summary: A cached, polite HTTP fetching library tested against a local fixture server.
requirements: A `Fetcher` wraps `requests.Session` with a timeout on every call, a User-Agent header and bounded retries with backoff on 429/5xx.
A disk or SQLite cache keyed by URL stores body, status and fetch time; entries expire after a configurable TTL and stale entries are refetched.
Conditional requests: when the server sent ETag/Last-Modified, the fetcher sends If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since and treats 304 as a cache refresh.
A parser extracts title, links and one structured record (for example product name and price) from the fixture site using BeautifulSoup or lxml.
Cache hits do not touch the network (asserted by counting requests on the fixture server).
Failures (timeouts, non-HTML content type, oversized bodies) raise typed exceptions and never poison the cache.
The clock is injectable so TTL tests need no sleeping.
deliverables: Library with `Fetcher`, `Cache` and `parse_*` modules
Local fixture server used by tests (http.server in a thread)
Container image that runs a scheduled scrape

grading.tests: Tests start a local HTTP fixture server that serves pages, ETags, 429 bursts and slow responses; nothing hits the real internet.
grading.quality: ruff check clean, mypy on the public API, pytest coverage >= 80% (pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80)
grading.deploy: Log of two scheduled runs where the second reports cache hits, plus the image build log.
hidden_test_ideas: The 2nd request within TTL causes zero server hits
After TTL expiry exactly one refetch occurs
A 304 response updates the timestamp without rewriting the body
A hanging server triggers the timeout, not a stuck test
A Retry-After header on 429 is honoured (with the fake clock)

guided.receives: Scaffold: typed stubs with docstrings and TODOs, a README task list and a visible pytest suite that names every behaviour.
guided.does: Fill in Fetcher and TTL Cache against one fixture site, then add ETag revalidation.

spec.receives: A written spec (the requirements list) and the public interface only; a small visible smoke test. The full hidden test suite runs when you submit or in CI.
spec.does: Implement the library from the spec and make parsers pluggable by registering a function per host; hidden tests add new hosts.

open.receives: A one-paragraph brief and the review rubric. No tests are provided: you write your own and you decide the design.
open.does: Build a polite crawler library: per-host rate limits, robots.txt compliance and an audit trail of what was fetched and why.
open.extension: Add robots.txt handling via `urllib.robotparser`, a per-host token-bucket delay, and a crawl report that lists blocked, cached and fetched URLs.
review_rubric: Network behaviour is safe: timeouts, retries, size limits
Cache correctness including revalidation and expiry
Politeness and legal awareness (robots, rate limits, User-Agent)
Pluggable parser interface with tests
Tests are hermetic and fast (no real sleeping, no internet)

deployment.free_tier: Build a small image and run it locally or in a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow (public repos have free minutes). Scrape only sites whose terms allow it, or your own fixture data.
deployment.teardown: Remove the workflow schedule or `docker rm` the container; delete the cache volume.

hints: Split policy from mechanism: Fetcher does HTTP, Cache does storage, a small orchestrator glues them, and a clock object is passed in.
Cache the response metadata you need for revalidation (ETag, Last-Modified), not just the body.
A fixture server should record every request so tests can assert on counts and headers.
Hash the URL for the cache key but store the original URL inside the entry to aid debugging.

projects.title: Bank System
projects.summary: An OOP bank with atomic transfers, an exception hierarchy and property-tested invariants.
requirements: Accounts hold balances in integer cents; `deposit`, `withdraw` and `transfer` reject non-positive amounts with `ValueError` subclasses.
Overdrafts are refused with `InsufficientFunds` unless the account type (checking with an overdraft limit) allows it.
`transfer(a, b, amount)` is atomic: on any failure neither account changes, and total money in the system is conserved.
A `SavingsAccount` accrues interest via an explicit `apply_interest(rate)` using banker-safe rounding documented in the README.
Every operation returns or records an immutable `Transaction` (id, timestamp, kind, amount, balance_after).
Frozen or closed accounts reject all mutating operations with a specific exception.
A hypothesis (or randomized) test asserts conservation of money over arbitrary operation sequences.
deliverables: Package with Account, CheckingAccount, SavingsAccount, Bank, exceptions
Unit tests plus property tests
Dockerfile that runs the test suite and a demo script

grading.tests: Visible tests cover the happy paths and each exception; hidden invariants use random operation sequences.
grading.quality: ruff check clean, mypy on the public API, pytest coverage >= 80% (pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80)
grading.deploy: Docker build log showing the test stage passing and demo output from `docker run`.
hidden_test_ideas: Sum of all balances is unchanged after any sequence of transfers
A failed transfer leaves both balances and both histories unchanged
Concurrent-looking sequences (interleaved ops) never yield negative balance on non-overdraft accounts
Balance always equals the initial balance plus the signed sum of the transaction log
Closing an account with a non-zero balance is refused

guided.does: Complete Account and the exception hierarchy, then implement atomic transfers against the visible tests.

review_rubric: Invariants are stated and enforced by design, not by luck
Exception hierarchy is meaningful and tested

Do the transfer as validate-both then mutate-both, or as a compensating rollback; decide and test which.
A property test can compare the system to a tiny model (dict of balances) applying the same operations.
Keep the transaction log the source of truth and derive balances from it in the extension.

projects.title: Async Link Checker
projects.summary: A concurrency-limited async crawler that reports broken links with correct timeouts and cancellation.
requirements: `linkcheck https://site/ --depth 2` crawls same-host pages and checks every link concurrently with an `asyncio.Semaphore` limiting in-flight requests to `--concurrency N`.
Each request has a total timeout (`asyncio.timeout` or client timeout) and a connect timeout; a hanging server never blocks the run beyond the timeout.
Results are classified: ok, redirect (with final URL), client error, server error, timeout, DNS/connection error; each URL is checked at most once.
HEAD is tried first with a GET fallback for servers that return 405/501 to HEAD.
The exit code is non-zero if any broken links are found; a JSON report lists source page, target URL, status and latency.
Cancellation is clean: Ctrl-C cancels outstanding tasks, closes the client and prints a partial report.
The maximum observed concurrency (measured by the fixture server) never exceeds N.
deliverables: CLI package with async core
Local fixture server with slow/flaky/redirecting endpoints for tests
Container image published locally or to GHCR

grading.tests: Tests run an aiohttp/uvicorn fixture site; pytest-asyncio verifies results and the concurrency ceiling.
grading.quality: ruff check clean, mypy on the public API, pytest coverage >= 80% (pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80)
grading.deploy: Container run log against the fixture site, with the JSON report attached.
hidden_test_ideas: Server-side counter of simultaneous connections never exceeds N
A 10 s hang with a 1 s timeout finishes in about 1 s
Redirect chains longer than the limit are reported, not followed forever
Duplicate links across pages are fetched once
KeyboardInterrupt equivalent (task cancel) leaves no pending tasks

guided.receives: Scaffold: typed stubs with docstrings and TODOs, a README task list and a visible pytest suite that names every behaviour.
guided.does: Complete the checker using `asyncio.gather` plus a semaphore for the fixed list of URLs.

spec.receives: A written spec (the requirements list) and the public interface only; a small visible smoke test. The full hidden test suite runs when you submit or in CI.
spec.does: Build the crawler from the spec using an `asyncio.Queue` and N workers so discovery and checking overlap.

open.receives: A one-paragraph brief and the review rubric. No tests are provided: you write your own and you decide the design.
open.does: Build a production-quality link checker: retries with jittered backoff, per-host limits and a report you would attach to a CI failure.
open.extension: Add retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient errors, per-host concurrency limits and a `--baseline` file that only fails on new broken links.
review_rubric: Concurrency is bounded and proven by a test
Timeout, cancellation and error classification are correct
Crawl logic avoids loops and duplicates
Reports are useful in CI (exit code, JSON, baseline)
Async tests are deterministic, not sleep-based

deployment.free_tier: Build a container and run it against your own docs site; optionally run it on a schedule in GitHub Actions (free minutes for public repos).
deployment.teardown: `docker rm`/`rmi` locally; remove the scheduled workflow.

hints: A semaphore bounds concurrency, but tasks are still created up front with `gather`; a queue with a fixed pool of workers bounds task count too.
Use `asyncio.timeout()` (Python 3.11+) or the client timeout object; test with a server that never responds.
Have the fixture server track current and maximum in-flight requests so the test can assert on it.
Wrap each worker in try/finally so cancellation always marks `queue.task_done()`.

projects.title: Plugin Task Runner
projects.summary: A DAG-based task runner with decorator registration, entry-point plugins and parallel execution.
requirements: Tasks are declared with a `@task(name, depends=[...])` decorator that registers them; duplicates and unknown dependencies raise clear errors at load time.
Additional tasks are discovered from installed packages through `importlib.metadata.entry_points(group="taskrunner.tasks")`.
The runner orders tasks with `graphlib.TopologicalSorter`; cycles produce a `CycleError` reported with the cycle path and exit code 2.
`tasks run build --dry-run` prints the plan without executing; `--only` and `--skip` filter safely without breaking dependencies.
A failing task marks dependents as skipped, continues independent branches and yields exit code 1 with a summary.
Parallel mode (`-j N`) runs ready tasks in a thread pool while respecting dependencies, and results are deterministic in the summary order.
Each task gets a context object (params, logger, outputs of dependencies) rather than using globals.
deliverables: Installable package with the runner and two example plugin packages
Plugin discovery tests using a temporary installed distribution or a fake entry-point set
Package published to TestPyPI or PyPI

grading.tests: Tests build in-memory graphs, monkeypatch `entry_points`, and assert order, skips and exit codes.
grading.quality: ruff check clean, mypy on the public API, pytest coverage >= 80% (pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80)
grading.deploy: `pip install` of the published package into a clean venv and a log of `tasks list` showing plugin tasks.
hidden_test_ideas: Diamond dependencies run the shared task exactly once
Failure in one branch does not stop an independent branch
Plugin with a broken import is reported and skipped, not fatal
Parallel run never starts a task before its dependencies finish
Output ordering is stable across runs

guided.receives: Scaffold: typed stubs with docstrings and TODOs, a README task list and a visible pytest suite that names every behaviour.
guided.does: Implement registration and a linear runner, then switch ordering to graphlib for a DAG.

spec.receives: A written spec (the requirements list) and the public interface only; a small visible smoke test. The full hidden test suite runs when you submit or in CI.
spec.does: Implement DAG execution, failure propagation and entry-point discovery from the spec; hidden tests use plugin fixtures.

open.receives: A one-paragraph brief and the review rubric. No tests are provided: you write your own and you decide the design.
open.does: Build a task runner suitable for a small team: parallel execution, caching by input hash and readable failure output.
open.extension: Add input-hash caching so a task is skipped when its declared inputs and dependency outputs are unchanged, plus a `--graph` command that emits Graphviz DOT.
review_rubric: Clean plugin boundary (entry points, versioning, isolation of failures)
Scheduling correctness under failure and parallelism
API design of the decorator and context
Usability: dry-run, filtering, error messages

Entry points are selected with `entry_points(group=...)` in Python 3.10+; test by patching the function rather than installing packages.
Keep the registry an object you can instantiate per test; a global dict leaks state between tests.

projects.title: SQL Query Builder / mini-ORM
projects.summary: A parameterised SQL builder and mini-ORM with an injection corpus and checksummed migrations.
requirements: A fluent builder (`Table("users").select("id","name").where(col("age") > 18).order_by("name").limit(10)`) compiles to `(sql, params)` with all values passed as bound parameters.
Identifiers (table and column names) are validated against the declared model or an allowlist and quoted correctly; they are never interpolated from raw user strings.
Supports SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE with WHERE combinators (and/or/not, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL) and correct parenthesisation.
Joins (INNER/LEFT) with aliases compile correctly and reject ambiguous column references.
A small `Model` layer maps rows to dataclasses and runs against sqlite3 via a `Session` object with transaction context manager.
A migration runner applies numbered scripts once, records them in a `schema_migrations` table and refuses to run out-of-order or modified applied scripts (checksum).
A corpus of injection strings (quotes, comments, stacked queries, unicode tricks) never changes the query structure.
deliverables: Library with builder, models, session and migrations
Injection test corpus and property tests comparing compiled SQL shapes
Wheel built with `python -m build` and installed in a clean venv

grading.tests: Tests execute against in-memory SQLite: result correctness, SQL text shape and an injection corpus checked structurally.
grading.quality: ruff check clean, mypy on the public API, pytest coverage >= 80% (pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80); mypy strict on the builder module
grading.deploy: Log of `pip install dist/*.whl` in a clean venv and a demo script running against SQLite.
hidden_test_ideas: Every injection string as a value leaves the SQL text identical and appears only in params
Hostile column names raise an error rather than quote-escape into a query
Changing an already applied migration is detected via checksum
OR/AND precedence is preserved with parentheses
Empty IN lists compile to a valid false condition

guided.does: Implement SELECT compilation with parameters and where-combinators from the scaffold; joins and migrations are provided as stubs to fill next.

projects.title: Self-healing Watchdog
projects.summary: A supervisor that probes, restarts with backoff, stops crash loops and escalates.
requirements: The watchdog launches a child service with `subprocess.Popen` and probes it (HTTP GET or TCP connect) every `interval` seconds with a timeout.

Restarts use exponential backoff with jitter, reset after a period of stable health, and stop after `max_restarts` in a window (crash-loop protection).
Escalation: after the crash-loop limit the watchdog stops restarting, writes a clear status file and exits non-zero or invokes a notification hook.
The watchdog handles SIGTERM/SIGINT itself by shutting down the child first, and SIGHUP to reload config.
Clock, sleep, probe and process launcher are injectable so tests need no real waiting.

projects.title: Canary/Shadow Serving
projects.summary: A router that splits, shadows and progressively promotes model versions with automatic rollback.
requirements: Two model versions (stable and candidate) run as separate Deployments behind a router service that splits traffic by configured weight with a deterministic hash of a request or user key (sticky per key).
Shadow mode sends a copy of each request to the candidate, discards its response, and records both outputs and latencies for comparison without affecting users.
Metrics per version (request count, error rate, latency percentiles, and a model-quality proxy such as prediction agreement) are exposed and stored.
A decision function compares candidate and stable over a window with minimum sample size and returns promote, hold or rollback; thresholds are configurable.
Automatic rollback sets candidate weight to 0 within a stated time when the error rate or latency SLO is breached, and logs the decision with its evidence.
Promotion steps traffic gradually (for example 5, 25, 50, 100) with a soak period at each step.
All decision logic is a pure, tested function separate from the Kubernetes plumbing.
deliverables: Router service, decision engine and model stubs
Kubernetes manifests for kind
Runbook: manual override, rollback and how to read the metrics

grading.deploy: Screenshot/log of a promotion that succeeds and a canary rolled back automatically after an injected fault.

Too few samples leads to hold, not promote
A latency spike for one window does not roll back unless persistent per rule

projects.title: Feature Store
projects.summary: A mini feature store with point-in-time joins, online serving and TTLs.
requirements: Features are declared in code or YAML (entity key, event timestamp column, value columns, TTL, source) and validated on load.

An offline store (Parquet or SQLite) holds historical feature values; `get_historical_features(entity_df, features)` performs a point-in-time join so each row only sees values at or before its event time (as-of join).
Leakage protection: values with a timestamp after the label time are never joined; a test with future-dated rows proves it.
An online store (SQLite or Redis) holds the latest value per entity; `materialize(start, end)` copies from offline to online idempotently.
`get_online_features(entity_ids)` returns values with their timestamps and treats values older than the TTL as missing.
The same transformation code is used for offline and online computation, and a skew test compares both paths on the same inputs.
Late-arriving data and backfills are handled: rematerialising a window gives the same online state.
deliverables: Library with definitions, stores, materialization
Leakage and skew test suites
Docker Compose demo with Redis

grading.tests: Tests build small event tables and label tables and assert the joined values against hand-computed expectations; property tests permute input order.
grading.quality: ruff check clean, mypy on the public API, pytest coverage >= 80% (pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80); property-based tests with hypothesis for join ordering
grading.deploy: Compose demo output: historical training frame, materialise, online lookup and TTL expiry.
hidden_test_ideas: A label at t=10 never sees a feature value stamped t=11
Row order of the entity dataframe does not change the result
Materialising the same window twice yields identical online state
A value older than TTL returns null
Offline and online values for the same entity and time are equal

projects.title: Batch Inference DAG
projects.summary: An idempotent, backfillable batch inference DAG with validation gates and deterministic reruns.
requirements: A pipeline with tasks `extract -> validate -> predict -> write` is defined as an Airflow DAG (or Prefect flow) with explicit dependencies and retries with backoff.
Each run is parameterised by a logical date/partition; input and output paths are derived from it (for example `dt=2025-03-01`), not from "now".
Tasks are idempotent: re-running a partition overwrites its output atomically (write to temp then rename) and never duplicates rows.
Rerun determinism: the same partition, model version and input produce byte-identical predictions (fixed seeds, sorted output).
A data-validation task fails the run on schema or volume anomalies before any prediction is written.
Backfill: `airflow dags backfill` (or the equivalent) over a date range processes partitions independently and in parallel up to a limit, and skips completed partitions.
The model version used is recorded in the output metadata and a manifest lists row counts and hashes.
deliverables: DAG definition, task code and tests
Local run environment (Docker Compose Airflow or kind)
Runbook: rerun, backfill and failure handling

grading.tests: Task functions are unit-tested pure functions; DAG-structure tests import the DAG and assert dependencies, retries and no import-time side effects; a rerun test runs a partition twice and diffs the outputs.
grading.quality: ruff check clean, mypy on the public API, pytest coverage >= 80% (pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80)
grading.deploy: Screenshot/log of the DAG run, a rerun producing identical hashes and a backfill of several dates.
hidden_test_ideas: Running a partition twice yields identical bytes and row counts

projects.title: Auto-retrain Loop
projects.summary: A simulated closed loop of drift detection, gated retraining and staged promotion.
requirements: A simulator generates a data stream with configurable drift (gradual and sudden) and delayed labels so the whole loop can be tested end to end deterministically.
Monitors (drift statistic, delayed-label performance) produce trigger events; triggers are debounced and rate-limited (cooldown, max retrains per window).
A retrain job builds a new candidate from a versioned dataset snapshot and registers it with lineage (data hash, code version, params) in a registry.
Gates decide promotion: candidate must beat the production model on a fresh holdout by a margin, pass fairness/latency/size checks and not regress on key slices.
Promotion is staged (shadow or canary) and reversible; a failed gate leaves production untouched and records why.
A manual mode (human approval) and an automated mode share the same code path so the difference is only who approves.
An end-to-end simulation test runs 30 simulated days and asserts the loop recovers accuracy after the drift event and never retrains more than the limit.
deliverables: System with monitor, trigger, trainer, gate and promoter components
Simulation harness and end-to-end tests
Kubernetes manifests or CronJobs for kind, and a design document

grading.tests: The end-to-end simulation asserts the sequence of events, accuracy recovery, cooldown compliance and that bad candidates never reach production.

grading.deploy: Log of a simulated drift event flowing through trigger, retrain, gates and canary on kind.
hidden_test_ideas: Sudden drift triggers exactly one retrain, not a storm

projects.title: Serverless Image Pipeline
projects.summary: S3 to SQS to Lambda thumbnails with fan-out, DLQ and idempotent processing, tested on LocalStack.
requirements: An upload to an S3 `incoming/` prefix triggers a notification to an SQS queue (or directly to Lambda) and a Lambda function creates thumbnails in a `processed/` prefix.
Fan-out: one upload produces several sizes (for example 128, 512 and 1024 px) either in one function or by a second queue and workers.
The queue has a redrive policy: after `maxReceiveCount` failures a message goes to a dead-letter queue, and a test proves a poison image lands there.
The handler is idempotent: processing the same message twice yields the same output keys without duplicates (the queue delivers at least once).
The Lambda uses partial batch responses (`batchItemFailures`) so one bad message does not fail the whole batch.
IAM roles are least-privilege (read incoming, write processed, send to DLQ, write logs only) and the infrastructure is code (Terraform, SAM, CDK or CloudFormation).
Image code is a pure function tested without AWS; an end-to-end test runs against LocalStack or moto and asserts outputs.

projects.title: Idle-Resource Cost Optimizer
projects.summary: Finds idle AWS resources, estimates savings and safely tags/stops them. Related lab: devops-aws-audit-moto.
requirements: The tool paginates through EC2 instances, EBS volumes and Elastic IPs across a list of regions using boto3 paginators.

Idle detection uses explicit rules: stopped instances older than N days, unattached volumes, unassociated Elastic IPs, and running instances with average CPU below a threshold from CloudWatch metrics.
A savings estimate per finding uses a price table you pass in (instance type, volume size and type); prices are input data, not hard-coded guesses.
`report` prints Markdown/JSON and never modifies anything; `tag` adds an audit tag (`idle-candidate=<date>`) and `stop` acts only on resources whose tag is older than a grace period.
Protected resources (tag `keep=true`, production tags, autoscaling members) are never touched, and every action supports `--dry-run` (default) versus `--execute`.
API throttling and `ClientError` are handled with backoff, and permissions errors in one region do not abort the others.
The time source is injectable so age calculations are testable; tests use moto to create fixtures.
deliverables: CLI package
moto-based test suite with fixture builders

projects.title: IAM Least-Privilege Audit
projects.summary: An offline IAM policy auditor that finds wildcards and escalation paths and gates CI.
requirements: The tool parses IAM policy documents (identity-based, both inline and managed, single or list `Statement`, `Action`/`NotAction`, `Resource`/`NotResource`) and reports invalid JSON with a location.
Detects `Effect: Allow` with `Action: "*"`, service wildcards (`s3:*`), `Resource: "*"`, `NotAction` allows and `NotResource` without justification.
Flags privilege-escalation-capable actions (for example `iam:PassRole` on `*`, `iam:CreatePolicyVersion`, `sts:AssumeRole` on `*`, `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode`) with an explanation.
Trust policies are checked: a `Principal: "*"` or an account-wide principal without conditions is flagged.
Each finding has a severity, the statement index, a reason and a suggested narrower policy (for example split `s3:*` into the needed list-and-get actions on named buckets).
A fix mode produces a proposed tightened policy from a list of actions actually used (from access logs or a usage export) and never widens permissions.

projects.title: Multi-region Failover Drill
projects.summary: A two-region service with DNS failover, measured RTO/RPO and a rehearsed runbook.
requirements: A stateless service and a data store are deployed in two regions with Terraform modules parameterised by region (primary and secondary).
Route 53 failover records (or weighted with health checks) point at the primary and the secondary; a health check watches a `/healthz` endpoint that verifies real dependencies.
Data replication is chosen deliberately (for example DynamoDB global tables, S3 cross-region replication or Aurora Global Database) and its lag (RPO) is measured and documented.
The DR posture is implemented at one level and the upgrade to the next is documented: pilot light (data replicated, compute off), warm standby (scaled-down compute), active-active.

A scripted outage (block the primary health check or scale primary to zero) triggers failover; the script records timestamps for detection, DNS change and first successful request, giving a measured RTO.
A runbook lists decision points, commands, verification steps and rollback (failback) with owners, and is exercised by the drill.
Everything can be torn down with one command and a cost estimate for a drill hour and a month of idle standby is included.
deliverables: Terraform for both regions
Drill script with timing output
Runbook (markdown) and post-drill report with RTO/RPO measurements

grading.tests: Automated drill test in a sandbox measures time to first successful request after the simulated outage and compares with the stated RTO; static checks confirm health check and replication configuration.

grading.deploy: Drill report showing timestamps and the measured RTO/RPO, plus the teardown confirmation.

Data written just before the outage is available after failover within the stated RPO
Failback does not lose writes made in the secondary

Destroy leaves no billable resources

review_rubric: Strategy fits the stated RTO/RPO and budget
Measured evidence from a real drill

deployment.free_tier: This project needs a real AWS account with two regions and can cost money (health checks, replication, NAT gateways, load balancers, standby compute); it is not free-tier friendly. Use the smallest footprint, set budget alerts and run the drill in a short window. DNS TTL and resolver caching make failover slower than the health-check interval alone suggests.
deployment.teardown: `terraform destroy` in both regions; verify no load balancers, NAT gateways, replicated tables, buckets or Route 53 health checks remain; delete the budget last.

hints: DNS TTL is part of your RTO: a 300 s TTL means clients may take minutes to move even after Route 53 flips.
Health checks that only test the process will keep sending traffic to a region whose database is down; check dependencies.
RPO is bounded by replication lag; measure it under load, not idle.
Practise failback too. Many teams fail over successfully and then cannot return safely.
